member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Common.CacheLinePadded
member.summary: Pushes the fields a derived class declares into the second cache line, so that an object whose hot state is written by one thread never shares a cache line with its neighbour.
member.remarks:
The padding is split across two places because of two runtime restrictions: the runtime ignores on a class that holds references, and it rejects explicit layout on a generic type. The leading half therefore lives here, in a non-generic base whose only field sits at the end of the first cache line, and the trailing half is a field declared by the most derived class — the runtime places it after every base-class field. With both halves in place a padded object is at least one cache line longer than its own fields at each end, which is what keeps neighbouring objects out of each other's line once the garbage collector compacts objects that different threads allocated next to each other.
This is layout only. No member, default value or observable behaviour changes; the cost is the padding bytes on the few long-lived instances that opt in.

member.summary: Which idle object a borrow is served (2.8; extended by G-21). The idle list is kept in return order — the tail is always the most recently returned object — and no strategy ever reorders it. and therefore only choose an end of that list, while and walk it and pick a node; either way the list itself, and so the end the eviction scan samples, is left exactly as it was.

member.summary: First in, first out (default): the borrow takes the oldest returned object, that is the head of the idle list. This reproduces the behaviour of every release before the switch existed.

member.name: F:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateBorrowStrategy.Lifo
member.summary:
Last in, first out: the borrow takes the most recently returned object, that is the tail of the idle list. Handing back the object that came in last keeps a small working set hot in the CPU caches, and it is the order the reference CHOPIN pool hard-codes. Objects that are never picked stay at the head and age out through the ordinary eviction rules.
Applies to the general-purpose engine only. The lean fast path keeps no ordered idle list, so a lean pool rejects this value at build time rather than accepting a knob it cannot honour.

member.name: F:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateBorrowStrategy.Lru
member.summary:
Least recently used: the borrow takes the object that was borrowed longest ago — the smallest , with an object that has never been borrowed (timestamp zero) ranking lowest of all. This orders by borrow where orders by return, so an object borrowed early and returned late is served before one borrowed and returned quickly; the two agree only while every object is returned in the order it was borrowed.
The idle list is not reordered and the borrow walks it, so the eviction sampler keeps seeing the end it has always seen. Applies to the general-purpose engine only: the lean fast path keeps no ordered idle list, the lock-free store keeps no order at all, and the per-shard front tier is consulted before the shard so it cannot take part in an order either — a pool that combines this value with any of the three fails the build rather than honouring it in part.

member.name: F:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateBorrowStrategy.Priority
member.summary:

Objects the comparer calls equal are served oldest-returned first, the same end would have served, so the order is deterministic without the comparer having to be a total one.
The comparer is a builder-time argument rather than an option, because is not generic: selecting this value without supplying one fails the build. The idle list is not reordered, so the eviction sampler is unaffected. Like this is unavailable on the lean fast path, on the lock-free store and alongside the per-shard front tier.

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateCircuitBreakerOptions
member.summary: Circuit-breaker settings for the pool-level availability guard, used when is on.
member.remarks:
The breaker protects the pool as a whole rather than an individual object. When the dependency behind the pool fails, the application reports it with SetUnavailable; once the configured number of consecutive failures has accumulated, the pool marks itself unavailable and every further acquire fails immediately instead of handing out objects that are likely to be broken. While unavailable, a background probe runs on the pool's shared timer — the probe is the only background work the breaker adds, it starts only when the breaker trips and stops as soon as the pool recovers.
Two trip rules are available and either one is enough: a consecutive failure streak () and, when enabled, a failure percentage over a sampled window ( together with ). Recovery is either a single probe or a run of healthy probes (), and an explicit SetAvailable closes the breaker at once whatever the run has reached.

member.name: P:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateCircuitBreakerOptions.FailureThreshold
member.summary:
Number of consecutive reported dependency failures that trips the breaker.
Default value: (3).
member.remarks:
Purpose: absorbs transient hiccups — a single failure report does not take the pool out of service.
Special case: the streak counts consecutive reports without an intervening recovery. It is reset to 0 by SetAvailable (explicitly, or through a successful probe), so a pool that recovered needs repeated fresh failures before it trips again; sporadic failures spread over a healthy lifetime also accumulate, and an application that knows the dependency is fine can call SetAvailable at any time to clear the pending streak. Set it to 1 to trip on the first report.
Boundary: values below 1 are normalized to 1 by .

member.name: P:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateCircuitBreakerOptions.FailurePercentageThreshold
member.summary: Failure percentage, in percent, at which the breaker trips. Default value: (0, the rule is off).
member.remarks:
Purpose: complements where a consecutive streak is a poor signal — a dependency that fails one call in three never produces three failures back to back, yet it is plainly broken. A report is either a failure (SetUnavailable) or a success (SetAvailable); the ratio is taken over the reports collected since the breaker last changed state, because the window is reset on every trip and every recovery. It therefore describes the current run of the breaker rather than the pool's whole lifetime.
Special case: the two trip rules are alternatives, never a conjunction — the breaker trips when either the streak or the percentage is reached, so turning this on cannot make a pool harder to protect. The ratio is only evaluated once reports have been collected.
Boundary: values below 0 (and NaN) are normalized to 0, values above 100 to 100, by .

member.summary: A borrow that returns itself, as a value type: the object taken from the pool is held by this lease, and disposing the lease puts it back exactly once. It is the allocation-free counterpart of — same lifetime rules, same return path, no heap object.

remarks.para: Obtain one through — the four AcquireLeased / AcquireLeaseAsync overloads are the only producers. Nothing else produces a lease, so the lifetime is unambiguous: the caller owns it, and the object it holds is unusable once the lease ends.

Which scope should I use? Both return the object on every path, including the exception paths, and both run the identical return path (validation, policy hooks, background eviction). They differ in one respect: this lease is a value type kept on the stack or in the calling frame, so acquiring one does not allocate, while is a class and costs one allocation per borrow. Reach for this lease on hot paths and in loops; reach for the scope when you need to pass the lease to a method that outlives the frame, store it in a field, hand it across an async boundary as an object, or otherwise need to treat it as a reference.

Disposal is idempotent. A lease represents one borrow, so returning must happen exactly once — a second call is deliberately a no-op rather than a second return, because double-returning the same object would let two borrowers share it later. The single-call guarantee holds even if several threads dispose the same lease concurrently, through an atomic claim.

Why this is a mutable struct rather than a ref struct. A ref struct cannot live across an await boundary: the compiler rejects it (CS4007), because the borrowed object would then have no defined owner while the continuation is pending. That makes its asynchronous disposal unreachable in practice, which would be a capability regression against , whose asynchronous disposal the 2.9 work added. Keeping the type a plain mutable struct preserves every capability of the scope — including await using and borrows that span an await — while still removing the per-borrow allocation. The price is the one guarantee a ref struct gave for free: this lease can be boxed, so putting one in a field or an object reference is allowed by the compiler and allocates then. It stays a value type in the normal using / await using flow. A readonly struct would not work either: the once-only return claim needs , and taking a field of a readonly struct by reference is rejected (CS8340).

It is the third constraint on the borrow path, next to the two that already exist: a shard's capacity bounds the objects the pool holds (idle plus borrowed, derived from ), and the reject policy decides what happens when no object is free. Neither of them caps how many borrowers may be in flight at once when the pool is large, so a pool sized for memory rather than for a downstream dependency will happily hand out every object it owns — and a database, a socket peer or a remote service behind those objects sees the whole burst at once. What happens at the ceiling is decided by , exactly as it decides a miss — the ceiling is a second reason for the same decision, not a separate policy: Abort refuses the request outright, Block waits until a borrower returns an object, and BlockTimeout waits for before giving up. The two creation policies are the deliberate exception: CreateNew and CreateOnDemand both wait instead of creating, because an object created to satisfy the request would be an object out on loan, which is precisely what the ceiling forbids. member.name: P:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayatePoolOptions.EnableLockFreeStorage
member.summary:

Purpose: the shard free list is the one lock the general-purpose borrow and return paths take, and one SpinLock per shard is what a burst of borrowers landing on the same shard contends on. With this switch on, an idle object sits in a slot the wrapper owns and is taken, or claimed for destruction, by a single Interlocked.CompareExchange on that slot — so a borrow or a return that finds the object never enters the shard lock, and neither does the eviction / idle-validation claim.

A slot array has no order to keep — a wrapper owns its slot for as long as it is parked — so the sequence a borrow walks is the slot layout, not the sequence the returns happened in. The eviction sampler's "oldest idle first" preference goes the same way: an object past or is still reclaimed when it is sampled, but the sample is no longer age-ordered. Correctness of both limits is unchanged.
For that reason the combination with = Lifo is refused at build time rather than silently downgraded to Fifo: an explicit request for an order the backend cannot honour fails the build, exactly as the lean fast path refuses a borrow order it cannot honour. A pool that never asked for anything holds the default Fifo and simply builds.
Special case: the slot array is sized when the shard is built, so a pool with this backend on refuses a ReloadConfig that would raise past that size — lowering it stays allowed. The same rejection the lean fast path makes for its own construction-sized retention buffer.

member.name: P:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayatePoolOptions.EnableThreadLocalFrontSlot
member.summary:

Default value: false (every borrow starts at a shard).
member.remarks:
Purpose: the steady-state borrow/return cycle of a single thread is "take the object I returned a moment ago". A per-thread slot turns that cycle into one compare-exchange on a field only this thread touches, and skips the shard walk entirely; a miss falls through to the unchanged shard path, which is the lock-free store when is on and the spin-lock free list when it is not.

The shared layer then starves with objects sitting in it. A slot therefore records whether its thread has borrowed, and a return from a thread that has not takes the ordinary shard path.

This is a storage shape, not a bookkeeping switch, so the feature profiles leave it alone; lean mode does force it off, for the same reason as .
Boundary: boolean switch. Off by default; each parked object costs one atomic on the return path and one on the borrow that hits it, in exchange for skipping the shard path.

remarks.para: The interface is deliberately separate from and is probed with is at construction, exactly as the asynchronous contract is. A policy that does not implement it compiles unchanged and pays one null test on the destroy path, and a policy that does implement it keeps its implementation untouched. Adding the two members to the main interface instead would have forced every implementer in the wild to add them.

The two hooks partition the reasons rather than overlapping: a validation failure arrives through OnValidationFailed, and every other destruction arrives through OnEvict with its . A policy that wants one entry point can route the first into the second itself.

Both hooks run before the object is torn down, so the value is still alive when the observer sees it, and both run exactly once per object: they sit behind the same idempotent claim that makes fire once. An exception thrown by either is logged and swallowed -- a misbehaving observer must not turn a destruction into a leak, or abort the drain that was in progress.

Different objects can be destroyed concurrently, so these callbacks can run concurrently too. An observer that updates shared state must provide its own synchronization; the pool serializes neither the callbacks nor the policy's other lifecycle methods.

The hooks are synchronous by design, on the same reasoning the asynchronous contract uses for Validate and OnAcquire: they are notification and bookkeeping, not I/O. A pool whose policy also implements IHayateAsyncObjectPolicy<T> is still observed through these members.

Coverage is the engine's, not a promise: the general-purpose engine reports every reason it can distinguish, while the lean fast path keeps no per-object state and never validates, so it reports the reasons it can judge and never reports . A drain reports even though it deliberately does not run -- the two are independent contracts.

This interface is available on every target. The netstandard2.0 and net48 builds do not support default interface methods, which is why the contract is a separate interface rather than two defaulted members on the main one.
